title: PR #173: Bump the "examples" group with 2 updates across multiple ecosystems

Changelog

Sourced from github.com/lestrrat-go/jwx/v3's changelog.

v3.4.0 23 Oct 2026

  • [jwe] jwe.Decrypt now tries each key provider in turn and moves on to the next one when a provider returns an error, as jws.Verify does. For example, jwe.WithKeySet with a set that has no usable key, followed by a working jwe.WithKey, decrypts with the working key. If no key works, the returned error wraps the last failure, so errors.Is can find it. (#2385)

  • [jwe] JSON serialization of a JWE now always includes the ciphertext member, jwe.Parse now accepts an empty ciphertext, and jwe.Decrypt now returns an empty payload for it. A JWE that encrypts an empty plaintext with AES-GCM therefore round-trips through jwe.Encrypt(..., jwe.WithJSON()), jwe.Parse, json.Marshal, and jwe.Decrypt. A missing, null, or non-string ciphertext is still rejected, and the iv and tag members must still be non-empty. (#2387)

  • [jwe] jwe.Decrypt now rejects a message whose tag or iv is not exactly the length the content encryption algorithm uses. Bytes can no longer be moved between ciphertext and tag to produce a different message that still decrypts. (#2387)

  • [jwe] JSON serialization of a JWE now writes the shared unprotected header as a JSON object, as RFC 7516 requires. A JWE with a shared unprotected header therefore round-trips through jwe.Parse, json.Marshal, jwe.Parse, and jwe.Decrypt. (#2389)

  • [jwt] jwt.WithNumericDateFormatPrecision now applies when a token is serialized. It covers the exp, iat, and nbf claims of jwt.Token, and those claims plus updated_at in openid.Token. Previously the option never had any effect on serialized tokens, which always wrote these claims as whole seconds.

    With a precision above 0, a date that has a fraction is written as a JSON number with up to that many fractional digits. Extra digits are rounded down, toward the earlier time, and trailing zeros are removed. At precision 3, an iat of 2000000000.123456789 is written as 2000000000.123, and 2000000000.1 as 2000000000.1. A date with no fraction is written as an integer, and output at the default precision of 0 is unchanged. Callers who set a precision above 0 will see fractional dates in their tokens, in the bytes jwt.Sign signs, and in what jwt.Equal compares. (#2410)

  • [jwt] NumericDate claims such as exp, iat, and nbf now parse negative values, which are dates before 1970, with or without jwt.WithNumericDateParsePedantic(true). The sign covers the fraction too, so -1.5 is one and a half seconds before the epoch. Fractional digits beyond jwt.WithNumericDateParsePrecision are rounded down, toward the earlier time, the same way serialization rounds: at the default precision of 0, -1.5 parses as -2. Positive values parse as before.
